title: Post-operative VTE prophylaxis
subtitle: Assess every patient, balance clot against bleed

sources.org: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
sources.title: Venous thromboembolism in over 16s: reducing the risk of hospital-acquired deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism (NG89)
Prevention of VTE in nonorthopedic surgical patients: Antithrombotic Therapy and Prevention of Thrombosis, 9th ed
American Society of Hematology 2019 guidelines for management of venous thromboembolism: prevention of VTE in surgical hospitalized patients

sources.org: American Society of Regional Anesthesia and Pain Medicine (ASRA)
sources.title: Regional anesthesia in the patient receiving antithrombotic or thrombolytic therapy, fourth edition

red_flags.text: Calf swelling, unexplained tachycardia, pleuritic chest pain, hypoxaemia or collapse after surgery: suspect deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism and investigate.
Active bleeding, a falling haemoglobin or a high-risk haemostatic situation: reconsider pharmacological prophylaxis.
An epidural or spinal catheter in place: the timing of every anticoagulant dose and of catheter removal matters.
Thrombocytopenia developing 5 to 10 days after starting heparin: heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.
A patient whose VTE risk assessment was never done or never repeated.

do_now.text: Assess VTE and bleeding risk for every surgical patient on admission, using a recognised tool, and record it.
Reassess at the consultant review and whenever the clinical situation changes.

Abdominal surgery with VTE risk outweighing bleeding risk: mechanical prophylaxis from admission until mobility is no longer significantly reduced, and pharmacological prophylaxis for a minimum of 7 days if bleeding risk is low.
Extend pharmacological prophylaxis to 28 days after major cancer surgery in the abdomen.

assess.text: Score VTE risk with the Caprini score in general and abdominal-pelvic surgery, as used by ACCP to grade prophylaxis.

Patient bleeding risk: active bleeding, acquired or inherited bleeding disorders, concurrent anticoagulants, thrombocytopenia, uncontrolled hypertension, and procedures with high bleeding consequences.
Renal function, weight and platelet count, which determine the agent and dose.
Suspected DVT or PE: assess clinical probability before testing.

investigate.text: Baseline full blood count, renal function and coagulation before starting pharmacological prophylaxis.
Platelet count monitoring where heparin-induced thrombocytopenia is a concern per local protocol.
Compression ultrasound or CT pulmonary angiography for suspected VTE; do not wait for symptoms to settle.

resuscitate.text: Caprini very low risk: early and frequent ambulation. Low risk (1 to 2): mechanical prophylaxis. Moderate risk (3 to 4): low-molecular-weight heparin, low-dose unfractionated heparin, or mechanical prophylaxis if bleeding risk is high.
Caprini high risk (5 or more): pharmacological prophylaxis plus mechanical prophylaxis unless bleeding risk is high; extended prophylaxis after abdominal or pelvic cancer surgery.
Where pharmacological prophylaxis is contraindicated, use mechanical methods such as intermittent pneumatic compression, and add the drug when bleeding risk falls.
Neuraxial catheters: leave at least 12 hours after a prophylactic dose of low-molecular-weight heparin before insertion or removal, and give the next dose no sooner than 4 hours after removal.

definitive.text: Low-molecular-weight heparin is the usual pharmacological agent; adjust for renal function and weight per local protocol.
Do not offer anti-embolism stockings to patients with suspected or proven peripheral arterial disease, severe peripheral neuropathy, or skin conditions that stockings would damage.
Encourage early mobilisation and adequate hydration as part of every prophylaxis plan.
Give the patient verbal and written information about VTE, prophylaxis at home, and how to administer injections if extended prophylaxis is prescribed.

escalate.text: Haematology for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, previous VTE on prophylaxis, thrombophilia or very high bleeding risk.
Anaesthesia before any anticoagulant dose change in a patient with a neuraxial catheter.
Senior surgeon if bleeding risk is uncertain after major surgery; the decision to withhold prophylaxis should be explicit and dated.

notes: Hospital-acquired VTE is one of the commonest preventable causes of death after surgery. The step that fails most often is the reassessment, not the first assessment.
Most post-operative pulmonary emboli occur in patients whose risk was known. Extended prophylaxis after abdominal cancer surgery is the most commonly missed element.
Mechanical prophylaxis buys time when bleeding risk is high. It is not a substitute for adding the drug once that risk falls.
